Lublin New Jewish Cemetery

Jewish Cemetery · Lublin, Poland

Not demolished. Lublin's new Jewish cemetery began with a land purchase in 1829, with burials starting the following year; it grew from an initial 3.66 hectares to 8.6 hectares by the 1930s as it expanded gradually northward. Alongside traditional stelae, it held unusually varied funerary art — obelisks, sculpted broken trees, piled rocks — and two brick ohels, one honoring the Ejger rabbinic dynasty of Lublin's Hasidim and the other honoring Rabbi Jehuda Meir Szapira, founder of the Daf Yomi global Talmud-study cycle and the renowned Chachmei Lublin Yeshiva. As ghetto deaths mounted during WWII, the cemetery was expanded by 2.5 hectares in 1940, and over 6,000 people were buried there before the ghetto's liquidation; after 1942, the cemetery was almost completely destroyed, leaving only a wall fragment and a few tombstones. Reestablished after Lublin's 1944 liberation on the site of the former cemetery square, it remained in use for exhumed and reburied victims as late as 1990, and today includes two Holocaust memorials. Restoration funded by the Sara and Manfred Bass-Frenkel Foundation between 1988 and 1993 added an artistically designed fence and two architectural memorials; the cemetery also now stores tombstones recovered from around Lublin and the nearby towns of Wieniawa, Głusk, and Puławy.
